DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection (Thornbury DC)

**Verdict:** the service has to go ahead, since it's a statutory duty, and the cost table adds up. But three of the study's central conclusions contradict its own figures:

- **Participation in flats was not similar to houses.** It was 21% against 66%.
- **Treatment can't all be local.** Brookfield can take about 1,800 tonnes a year, while the study projects about 3,290.
- **"Fully funded" doesn't survive correcting the participation figure.** That correction alone pushes the net cost above the allocation, before any of the gaps in the cost table are counted.

Cabinet should approve the roll-out in principle and the vehicle order. Flats, treatment capacity and funding need revised plans before the full figures go to them.

## What checks out

- **Table 1 rates:** 2,112/3,200 = 66%; 168/800 = 21%; 2,280/4,000 = 57%.
- **Table 2:**
  - Vehicles: 6 × £165,000 ÷ 7 = £141,400
  - Crews: 12 × £34,000 = £408,000
  - Total: £733,400
- **Disposal saving:** £112 − £38 = £74 per tonne, and 3,290 t × £74 ≈ £243,000.
- **Net cost:** £733,400 − £243,000 ≈ £490,000, which the £520,000 provisional allocation covers *as calculated*.

## 1. Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses

Section 2 says participation was "broadly similar across housing types." The table beside it shows **66% for houses and 21% for flats**. Flats are about 20% of the district (§3), so roughly 10,400 households would sit at about a third of the participation rate. That is a strong case *for* a separate approach to flats, the opposite of the study's conclusion. Typical measures include:

- communal bins in bin stores
- working with landlords and managing agents
- more frequent supply of liners
- targeted communications

The decision about a uniform service should be reversed. Flats need a design and a budget line of their own.

## 2. The 64% participation rate has no source

§3 applies **64%**. The pilot's overall rate was **57%**. The pilot's share of flats (800/4,000 = 20%) also matches the district's, so 57% is the right figure to scale up without any adjustment.

Projecting houses and flats separately from the pilot rates:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 160 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That is about **420 tonnes below** the study's 3,290 t. The pilot also ran January to June, so seasonal variation and early enthusiasm may affect the full-year figure in either direction.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the projected tonnage

§4 says Brookfield will offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Even the corrected 2,870 t leaves about **1,070 tonnes a year** with no contracted destination. On the study's own projection the shortfall is about 1,490 t.

The next nearest plant is **46 miles away**, more than three times the distance. Its gate fee and the extra haulage are not in the study. So the claim that treatment is local (the author's description) holds for only about 60% of the tonnage until 2029.

This is open. It's settled by a quote from the 46-mile plant, or by other outlets: a transfer station with bulk haulage, or contract capacity elsewhere.

## 4. "Fully funded" isn't established

- **Corrected tonnage alone breaks the funding.**
  - Disposal saving at full rate: 2,870 t × £74 ≈ £212,000
  - Net cost: £733,400 − £212,000 ≈ **£521,000**
  - Provisional allocation: £520,000

  That figure also treats all 2,870 t as if it went to Brookfield at £38/t. The ~1,070 t above the cap will cost more to haul and possibly more at the gate, so the real saving is lower and the gap larger.
- **The allocation is provisional.** The author's description says the net cost is "fully covered"; §5 says the allocation is provisional. The amount, how long it lasts, and whether it is ongoing revenue funding or one-off money all need confirming.
- **Cost lines are missing,** despite "every cost line is shown":
  - **Crew on-costs.** Is £34,000 salary only, or does it include employer's National Insurance and pension contributions? If salary only, on-costs could add roughly a fifth to a quarter, around £80,000–£100,000.
  - **Cover** for sickness and holidays, and a spare vehicle.
  - **Supervision and management.**
  - **The dedicated phone line and web page** described in §6.
  - **Extra haulage** for tonnage above Brookfield's cap.
  - **A flats-specific service** (see section 1).

The likely position is **a net cost somewhat above the allocation**. The size of the gap is open until these are costed and the funding confirmed.

One trap to avoid in revising the figures: lower participation reduces the disposal saving, but not the collection cost. Rounds are set by the number of households to visit, not by tonnage. Don't scale the vehicles and crews down with the tonnage.

## 5. The timetable needs confirmation

- **Vehicle lead time.** December to March is a three-month lead time. That is short for specialist vehicles. Confirm it with the supplier in writing, since the whole timetable depends on it.
- **March is crowded.** Crew recruitment starts in February, with training and caddy delivery to all 52,000 households in March. That's tight but possible. Name who owns each step and set a fallback start date.
- **Treatment contracts.** Both the Brookfield contract and arrangements for the excess tonnage need to be in place before collections start in April.

## Smaller points

- **Pilot satisfaction (81%):** give the response rate. People who used the service are more likely to answer the survey.
- **Per-household figure:** the weighted average is 1.86 kg per participating household. It rounds to 1.9 correctly, but the separate figures for houses and flats should drive the projection.

## Suggested recommendation

1. **Approve the roll-out in principle and authorise the vehicle order now.** The duty is statutory, and the vehicles are needed under any design. Delay risks missing April 2027.
2. **Bring back to Cabinet by [date]:**
   - a separate service design and budget for flats;
   - a treatment plan for the tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800 t cap, with costs;
   - full costing, including crew on-costs, cover and customer contact;
   - confirmed new-burdens funding, with its amount and duration.
3. **Replace "fully funded" with the revised net cost against confirmed funding,** stating any shortfall openly.
